text: THE BRITISH ARMY.

label: text
text: IT'S MOST ADVENTUROUS YOUNG RECRUIT.

label: text
text: Stephen William Harvey, who has just enlisted in the 10th Hussars (Prince Henry's regiment now at Aldershot) would probably be justified in describing himself as the most travelled and experienced young recruit the British Army has ever had.

label: text
text:
These are the principal events in his varied career, though he will not be 24 until next November:
Joined the Canadian Army at 13, and was for long the youngest member of the fighting forces;

label: text
text: Fought at Ypres (1915), the Somme, and Viny Ridge before he was 15. Won the Military Medal and the Croix de Guerre. Wounded twice:

label: text
text: Went to Archangel with the Russian Expeditionary Force after the Armistice, imprisoned for nine months by the Bolsheviks. Nearly starved to death;

label: text
text: Returned to Canada; travelled to Australia first-class; was down and out; nearly starved again; worked a passage on a Canadian vessel; became ill. Was landed at Fiji to recover;

label: text
text: Again returned to Canada, worked his way across to Halifax, joined the Canadian Navy;

label: text
text: Invalid out, after 18 months' service; worked his passage to England, shipped as a steward on the Aorangi for Australia, afterwards sailed round the world; operated on at sea and nearly died again;

label: text
text: Has travelled 35,000 miles since January 2 of this year:

label: text
text: "I am joining up again at Aldershot on Wednesday," Mr. Harvey told a "Daily Chronicle" representative who found him at an ex-Service men's hostel in Duke Street, Manchester Square.

label: text
text: He is a fair, ruddy-faced boy, looking just a trifle older than his years, which is not surprising.

label: text
text: He seemed to find his adventures very amusing in the retrospect, but apologised for his smile, explaining that he had had 17 teeth count on Thursday. His latest exploit! "They wouldn't take me in the Army until my teeth were seen to," he said.

label: text
text: **I was rejected at Scotland Ward (recently - office) because of them, so I walked to Woolwich and tried there; but they said the same thing. It is by the kindness of Countess Roberts that I am getting a new set.**

label: text
text: "I first joined the Army," he said. "Because my two brothers and my sister were all in France. I tried to enlist at Winnipeg, where my butler was mayor for three years, I said I was 49, but they told me to go home and ask my mother when I would be 11. A good guess!

label: text
text:
"So I pumped a train and went to Montreal. I told them there that I was 18, and this went down he'll be because they took me.
"When we got to France, my sister, who was a nurse, recognised me one day. I pretend I didn't know her, but she went to my colonel and asked for me to be sent home. I asked him to let me stay, and he did.

label: text
text: "My two brothers were both killed and my sister died in France of influenza."

label: text
text:
BOLSHEVISTS PRISONER.
“I was wounded twice, in the arm, at Y presound in the head at Passehenware. Afterwards, in Russia, I was taken prisoner by the Bolsheviks and had a terrible time. We were herded in a barbed wire enclosure and fed upon black bread and water. Sometimes women used to throw food over the fence to us. One of them was caught and chibbed over the head with the butt end of a ritle. Once 25 of us were continued in a sort of dungeon with three of our dead. The American Red Cross got me released at last, and I went back to Canada. Soon afterwards, my father and mother died. I booked a first-class passage to Australia with a little money that came to me, but I could get no work there, and was soon down and out, sleeping in the open.

label: text
text: "When I signed on as deck hand in the 'Canadian Skirmisher' to go back to Canada, I was so ill on the way that I nearly died. Wireless calls for medical help from other ships were sent out, but without avail. Finally, the ship's course was specially diverted, and I was put 'ashors at Suva, in the Fiji Islands. Afterwards, I recovered and returned to Canada. Since then I have been round the world."

label: text
text: Mr. Harvey has been presented to the King once and to the Prince of Wales twice. Of all the places he has seen he likes Honolulu the best. In London his chief enjoyment is to watch the Guards at drill.

label: text
text: He employed every expedient he knew to make the kettle 'boil. He burnt up a great quantity of wood without success. He almost demolished the kitchen in an unfortunate experiment with paraffin. Finally, to his chagrin, he was obliged to call his wife. She showed him a scheme he had not thought of at all. She put some water in the kettle.

label: paragraph_title
text: LETTERS TO A LORD.

label: text
text: A BLACK MAILER SENT TO

label: text
text: Sentence of nine months imprisonment in the second division was passed by Mr. Justice Salter, at the Central Criminal Court on June 18 on Samuel Arthur Taylor, 25, inquiry agent; who pleaded "Guilty" to a charge of attempting to obtain money from Lord Terrington by threatening to publish libels on Lord and Lady Terrington.

label: text
text:
Mr. Percival Clarke, for the prosecution, said the first letter was sent by the prisoner to Lord Terrington on May 11, and in it he asked for £95, pretending that he had got information in his possession for which he had received an offer from some other person, and he asked that if Lord Terrington decided to have the information, withheld he should place a visiting card in his window. Lord Terrington saw the police on the matter, and, acting on their instructions, put a card in his window, and later sent a letter to the address which the prisoner gave. The prisoner was arrested. He had since written from Brixton tendering his most sincere apologies to Lord and Lady Terrington. Counsel said the prisoner had no information at all which could reflect discredit on Lord or Lady Terrington, and this was merely an attempt on his part to extort money. Nothing was known against prisoner's character. This was not a sudden temptation on the part of a man who wanted money. When the prisoner's rooms were visited by the police they found that other letters had been written by him in the name of Watson in December, 1923, to Lord Terrington, in which he offered to sell Lord Terrington a book for £5. Lord Terrington did not know anything about this book or Watson, and he declined to buy the book. The prisoner stated that he was engaged to Lady Terrington's sister, but that was quite untrue. Flooring his sister he got to know Lady Terrington's sister. They were quite young. When Lady Terrington got to know of the acquaintance she threatened to make her sister a ward in Chaneery if it continued. That seemed to have upset the prisoner, and might explain why he wrote the letters.
Mr. Mafelom Carter, addressing the judge, on behalf of the prisoner, said he had not been in trouble before. He really could not account for why he wrote the letters. It was a cross and foolish mistake, and he desired to express his contribution.

label: text
text: Mr. Justice Salter, in passing sentence, said that blackmail was one of the vilest crimes known to the law. Lord and Lady Terrington had had the courage to come forward and discharge a public duty. Victims of blackmailers had not always that courage, and it was on that that blackmailers thrived. It had been called a foolish mistake on the prisoner's part, but he (Mr. Justice Salter) did not believe a word of that. It was a regular blackmailing scheme.

label: text
text: SYMPATHY OF MR. BERNARD SHAW.

label: text
text: Home papers contain much criticism of Mr. Epstein's panel in Hyde Park, one of the latest being that by G. Bernard Shaw, who writes in "The Times" as follows:—

label: text
text: On visiting the Bird Sanctuary on Saturday I found my way by an eloquently trampled path to a crowded railing, where I was confronted with a very remarkable sample—I use the word advisedly—of the great art of monumental wall sculpture which we rather feebly call bas relief. It was unquestionably the real thing, with all the power of stone and all the illusion of strenuous passion, and even movement, that live design can give. But it was a sample, and a ridiculously small one. It reminded me of a Quaker cloth merchant in my native Dublin, famous for the imperturbability of his temper. A young English officer, after making him take down every roll in his shop, at last selected a cloth, and gravely said he would take a halfpenny-worth of it. The unmoved Quaker cut out a piece the exact size of the halfpenny, wrapped it neatly in paper, and handed it respectfully to his customer.

label: text
text: It is evident that the Hudson memorialists, having collected what they could, were compelled to go to Mr. Epstein and say, "Please, sir, mother England wants four yards of your best monumental wall sculpture to put up in the Park for one of her famous sons." And Mr. Epstein solemnly delivered the four yards, which bear about the same proportion to what was needed as the Quaker's halfpennyworth of cloth to a suit of clothes. That is what comes of ordering a monument when you have only money enough to pay for a Christmas card. We get a monument to our national meanness in matters of high art. If it had been Wembley now! Next time, if we cannot afford to give Mr. Epstein carte blanche, we had better get the job done in the Euston Road in a thoroughly commercial manner.

label: text
text: I have a great deal of sympathy with the people who hate Mr. Epstein's sample. Some of them feel the reproach and the inadequacy for which they innocently blame Mr. Epstein. Some of them do not like monumental wall sculpture, and are in the grievous position of people who want a fox-trot and have a Beethoven symphony thrust into their ears. Why should not these people, who have a perfect right to their own tastes, have a monument and a bird sanctuary all to themselves? There is plenty of room in the Park for both. It need not cost much. There is a process called photo-sculpture, with an establishment in the West-End, by which very pretty reliefs can be made by the camera. If Miss Fay Compton or Miss Gladys Cooper would pose as Rima, with a stuffed pigeon on each wrist, the artist who touches up the photo-sculpture could throw in a few swallows, a robin, and a holly branch; and the result would be exactly what is wanted by the honest folk whose sense of beauty is outraged and mocked by Mr. Epstein's powerful proceedings. Why not please everybody when it is so easy?

text: ཡོད་པའི་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ཡོད་པ་ text: HERO WHO THREW SHELL OVERBOARD

label: text
text: The first Victoria Cross, ever awarded is a priceless relic left under the will of Mrs. Frances Russell Lucas, of Great Culverden, Tunbridge Wells, whose estate was proved at £10,637.

label: text
text: Mrs. Lucas was the widow of Admiral Charles David Lucas, who was the first man in either Navy or Army to win the V.C.

label: text
text: This was gained on June 20, 1854, when H.M.S. Hecla was bombarding Bomursunda fortress, in the Baltic. When the Hecla was within 500 yards of the principal fort a live shell, with the fuse burning, fell on the deck.

label: text
text: Lucas, who was then a'mite, picked up the shell in an instant and hurled it into the sea. Almost before it reached the water it exploded with a terrific roar.

label: text
text: Captain Hall of the Hecla, immediately promoted Lucas a lieutenant and three years later Queen Victoria decorated him with the Victoria Cross.

label: text
text: Mrs. Lucas was the daughter of Captain Hall, of the Hecla, afterwards. Admiral Sir William Hutchison Hall.
